questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Identify why blinding participants reduces bias in a pilot trial.
questions.stem: A ticket proposes a trial where the team cannot tell which build participants are testing. What is the main reason to blind participants?

options.text: Blinding stops participants changing their behaviour because they know they are being observed.
Blinding guarantees the measured effect will be large enough to be practically useful.
options.misconception: Believes blinding enlarges effects rather than protecting them

options.text: Blinding removes the need to keep a placebo group in the comparison.
options.misconception: Believes blinding can replace a genuine control group

options.text: Blinding ensures the two groups turn out identical in every measurable respect.
options.misconception: Believes blinding guarantees perfectly matched groups

questions.explanation: Participants who know they are watched often change how they behave, so the measured difference mixes the treatment effect with the reaction to being observed.
questions.hint: Think about behaviour changes when watched.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret how many separate test results a family of comparisons produces.

options.text: Thirteen, because the three family sizes are added together.
Six, because only the largest family matters for the release gate.
options.misconception: Believes only the biggest family counts towards the report

options.text: Three, because one p-value is reported per family rather than per test.
options.misconception: Believes a family yields one p-value whatever its size

options.text: Seven, because two of the three families can be merged before reporting.
options.misconception: Believes families can be pooled into a single p-value

questions.explanation: Every comparison contributes a p-value, so 4 + 6 + 3 = 13 appear in the report. Grouping families controls error rate but never reduces the number of tests performed.
questions.hint: Count each comparison, not each family.

questions.hint: Take one minus the no-error probability, raised.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain how Bonferroni adjustment limits the family-wise error rate.
questions.stem: A ticket asks the analyst to justify dividing the family alpha by the number of comparisons, in writing.

answer.exemplar: Each comparison keeps a chance of at most alpha divided by k of a false positive, so the chance of any false positive across the family stays at or below alpha overall. The price is a stricter threshold, so real but modest effects become harder to detect and the method consumes statistical power.

questions.explanation: Dividing alpha across the comparisons caps the chance of any false positive in the family at the family alpha, at the cost of a stricter threshold for every test.
questions.hint: Name the error rate it bounds.

options.text: Take each mean, subtract them, then divide by the pooled standard deviation.

options.misconception: Treats the standardised difference as a product of the means

options.text: Convert the means to percentages, then subtract them and divide by the range.
options.misconception: Confuses standardising a difference with percentaging the means

questions.explanation: A standardised mean difference divides the difference between the group means by a shared standard deviation, so the means come first and the divisor second.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Apply the shared variation concept to a latency comparison.

stimulus.body: Two server groups were compared: 60 hosts on the new release and 60 on the old one. Mean latency was 220 ms against 190 ms, and the within-group standard deviation was 45 ms in both groups. The analyst notes that the spread is shared rather than specific to either arm.

questions.stem: Given the ticket excerpt, why does the analyst emphasise that the 45 ms spread is shared across both groups?

options.text: It gives a common yardstick, so the 30 ms mean gap can be expressed in units of that spread.
It proves the two groups differ in their spread, so the mean gap needs no scaling.
options.misconception: Confuses a common spread with evidence of differing spread

options.text: It shows the two groups are identical, so the mean gap must be a measurement error.
options.misconception: Treats equal variation as proof that the means cannot differ

options.text: It means the 30 ms gap is large enough to skip calculating any standardised measure.
options.misconception: Believes a shared spread removes the need for standardisation

questions.explanation: A shared spread gives a common yardstick for the mean gap, 30 divided by 45. Sharing variation does not mean the groups are identical, and it never removes the need to standardise.
questions.hint: Think of the spread as a unit of measurement.

questions.learningObjective: Apply two steps to decide how to narrow a confidence interval.
questions.stem: A ticket asks how to narrow a confidence interval. First name the change that reduces the interval width, then name the change that keeps the estimate comparable.

options.text: Collect more independent observations and keep the same method and confidence level.
Report a smaller margin of error and drop the observations that widened the interval.
options.misconception: Believes trimming data and restating bounds narrows a real interval

options.text: Use the smallest sample in the ticket and widen the critical value for extra safety.
options.misconception: Believes a smaller sample with a wider bound gives a tighter interval

options.text: Treat the interval as a range of likely values and present it without any margin.
options.misconception: Believes restating the interval without a margin improves precision

questions.explanation: More independent observations shrink the standard error and therefore the interval width. Keeping the method and confidence level unchanged preserves comparability, while rounding or dropping observations only changes what is reported.

options.text: It measures how closely the two variables move together, without proving either one causes the other.

options.misconception: Confuses correlation with equality of measurement scales

options.text: It measures how consistently the two variables vary once sample size is corrected.
options.misconception: Believes correlation already corrects for the sample size used

questions.explanation: A correlation coefficient summarises the strength and direction of a linear relationship. It does not establish causation, does not compare absolute scales, and needs no sample-size correction of its own.

options.misconception: Calls any single difference random luck without considering the design

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why many comparisons raise the family-wise error rate.
questions.stem: A ticket asks for a written explanation of why running twelve checks on one release raises the risk of a misleading result.

answer.exemplar: Each check can produce a false positive at its own alpha level. Across twelve checks the chance that at least one is a false positive is far above any single alpha, because these are separate chances rather than one protected decision. Grouping them into a family and adjusting the threshold keeps the overall misleading-result risk where the team set it.

questions.explanation: False positives accumulate across checks, so the chance of at least one rises with the number of comparisons. Adjusting the threshold within a family keeps that overall risk at the agreed level.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Order the steps for applying a Bonferroni correction.
questions.stem: A ticket describes applying a Bonferroni correction to a set of comparisons. Which sequence of steps starts correctly?

options.text: Fix the family alpha, divide it by the number of comparisons, then test each result at that level.
Test each comparison at the full alpha, then divide the results by the comparison count.
options.misconception: Tests first and adjusts the family rate afterwards

options.text: Pick the smallest p-value, divide it by the number of comparisons, then declare it significant.
options.misconception: Adjusts only the smallest p-value instead of the threshold

options.text: Divide the observed effect by the comparison count, then check it against the family alpha.
options.misconception: Adjusts the effect size rather than the significance level

questions.explanation: The correction lowers the threshold each comparison is judged against, so the family alpha is divided first. Adjusting only the smallest p-value afterwards does not control the family rate.
questions.hint: Adjust the threshold, not the result.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Read a standardised mean difference out of a reported comparison.

stimulus.body: The release comparison reports a mean task time of 4.2 minutes for the new workflow against 4.8 minutes for the old one, with a pooled standard deviation of 0.6 minutes across both groups. A reviewer asks whether the gap is large enough to matter.

questions.stem: Given the excerpt, what standardised mean difference should the reviewer report?

options.text: About 1.0, since the 0.6 minute gap divided by the 0.6 minute spread equals one.
About 0.13, since the 0.6 minute gap divided by the 4.8 minute old mean gives the effect.
options.misconception: Divides the gap by the old group mean rather than the spread

options.text: About 0.08, since the 0.6 minute gap divided by the total sample of eight gives it.
options.misconception: Divides the gap by a sample count rather than a deviation

options.text: About 8.0, since the 4.8 minute old mean divided by the 0.6 minute gap gives it.
options.misconception: Inverts the ratio so a large effect reads as a large number

questions.explanation: The standardised mean difference divides the mean gap by the pooled standard deviation, so 0.6 over 0.6 gives 1.0. Dividing by a mean or a sample size uses the wrong denominator.
questions.hint: Divide the gap by the pooled spread.

questions.learningObjective: Apply shared variation to two steps of a group comparison.

options.text: You can express the mean gap in units of the spread, but you cannot conclude the groups are equivalent.
You can conclude the groups are equivalent, but you cannot express the mean gap in standard units.
options.misconception: Treats equal spread as proof of equivalent groups

options.text: You can compute the shared variance exactly, but you cannot compare the two group means at all.
options.misconception: Believes shared variance blocks any mean comparison

options.text: You can compare the group means directly, but you cannot use the spread for any standardisation.
options.misconception: Believes the spread cannot support standardisation

questions.explanation: Shared variation supplies a common denominator, so the mean gap can be standardised and compared across studies. It says nothing about equivalence, since equal spread with different means is possible.
questions.hint: A shared denominator is not a verdict.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the factor that most directly controls confidence interval width.
questions.stem: A ticket asks which single quantity the team should track to predict how wide a confidence interval will turn out.

options.text: The standard error of the estimate, since wider standard errors give wider intervals.
The sample size alone, since the standard error depends on nothing else at all.
options.misconception: Believes sample size fully determines the standard error

options.text: The observed effect size, since a larger effect always produces a wider interval.
options.misconception: Believes a bigger effect widens the interval

options.text: The confidence level alone, since the sample size and spread never matter.
options.misconception: Believes only the confidence level sets the width

questions.explanation: Interval width grows with the standard error and with the critical value of the confidence level. The standard error depends on spread and sample size, so no single other factor controls width alone.
questions.hint: Width is a multiple of the standard error.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret a reported correlation coefficient without overclaiming.

options.misconception: Reads a strong correlation as established causation

options.misconception: Treats correlation as a share of explained variation

options.text: Nine tenths of all changes to files are driven by how long the fix took.
options.misconception: Converts a coefficient straight into a percentage of causes

questions.explanation: A coefficient of 0.86 describes a strong positive linear association within the observed sample. It neither establishes causation nor converts directly into a percentage of variance explained.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why related tests are grouped into a family.
questions.stem: A ticket asks the analyst to explain why the flaky-test checks are grouped into one family before any correction is applied.

answer.exemplar: The checks in that family share a decision: if any one of them wrongly rejects the null, the release is blocked for the wrong reason. Grouping them states that the family shares one error budget, which lets the team apply a single correction instead of pretending each check is independent and harmless.

questions.explanation: Grouping says the checks share one decision and one error budget, so a single correction can be applied across them. Treating them as unrelated separate tests lets the family-wide chance of a false positive grow unchecked.
questions.hint: One family means one error budget.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Order the reasoning steps for judging family-wise error risk.
questions.stem: A ticket asks how the team should reason about the risk of a false positive across a family of checks. Which sequence begins correctly?

options.text: Count the checks, take each alpha, then combine those chances to find the family risk.
Take each alpha, count the checks afterwards, then ignore the family risk entirely.
options.misconception: Reverses the order of combining and counting the chances

options.text: Find the smallest p-value, divide it by the number of checks, then declare the family safe.
options.misconception: Judges the family by its single smallest p-value

options.text: Average the alpha levels of the checks, then compare that average with the family alpha.
options.misconception: Averages alphas instead of combining separate chances

questions.explanation: Family-wise risk comes from combining separate chances of a false positive, so the count and each alpha come first. A smallest p-value or an averaged alpha cannot give that risk.
questions.hint: Combine chances, do not average them.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Read a corrected threshold out of a reported family.

stimulus.body: A quality ticket compares four candidate algorithms on three metrics, giving twelve tests in total. The release policy allows a five per cent chance of a false positive across the whole family, and the analyst proposes dividing that budget by the number of tests.

questions.stem: Given the excerpt, what threshold should each of the twelve tests be judged against?

options.text: About 0.0042, because 0.05 divided by 12 is the per-test threshold.
About 0.05, because each test keeps the full family budget on its own.
options.misconception: Gives every test the entire family error budget

options.text: About 0.20, because the family budget is multiplied by the number of tests.
options.misconception: Multiplies the budget instead of dividing it

options.text: About 0.60, because the budget is divided among the four algorithm candidates.
options.misconception: Divides among candidates instead of among tests

questions.explanation: With twelve tests, the per-test threshold is 0.05 divided by 12, about 0.0042. Multiplying the budget, or dividing it among candidates rather than tests, would not bound the family error rate.
questions.hint: Budget divided by number of tests.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how a placebo condition controls for observer effects.

answer.exemplar: The placebo build gives both arms an identical ritual of installing, running and reporting, so any difference in results comes from the feature under test rather than from the extra attention that group receives. questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Compute the total width of a reported confidence interval.
questions.stem: A ticket reports a 95 per cent confidence interval for the mean defect count running from 7.2 to 8.8. What is the total width of that interval?
questions.explanation: The total width is the upper limit minus the lower limit, so 8.8 minus 7.2 gives 1.6. Half of that, 0.8, is the margin of error sitting either side of the estimate.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a correlation coefficient is computed from summarised data.
questions.stem: A ticket asks the analyst to describe, in writing, how the correlation for a batch of paired records is obtained from summary figures.

answer.exemplar: Start from the sums of x, y, xy, x squared and y squared over the paired records. Subtract the product of the sums of x and y from n times the sum of xy for the numerator, and use the two matching variance terms in the denominator, then take the square root of their product. Dividing gives a value between minus one and one that reflects the linear relationship only.

questions.explanation: The coefficient comes from the centred cross-product divided by the centred spreads of both variables, so a summary of sums is enough to compute it. It describes linear association only.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Order the steps for reducing observer effects in a pilot.
questions.stem: A ticket asks for the right order of changes when reducing observer effects in a usability pilot. Which sequence begins correctly?

options.text: Mask who receives which build, then run the session, then compare baseline behaviour across groups.
Run the session with full labels, then mask the build names afterwards so nobody knows what happened.
options.misconception: Masks only after the data are already collected

options.text: Ask participants afterwards whether they noticed the recording, then decide whether to mask anything.
options.misconception: Asks about awareness instead of preventing it

options.text: Compare the groups first, then mask the build names if the results look uneven.
options.misconception: Masks only when the results already look wrong

questions.explanation: Observer effects are prevented by masking the condition before data collection; a baseline check then shows whether the arms started alike. Masking afterwards cannot undo an effect already produced.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Read why related comparisons are grouped into one family.

stimulus.body: A rollout ticket compares the new scheduler against the old one across three separate workloads, and the analyst treats those three comparisons as one family because they feed the same go or no-go decision. Each comparison is run at the usual five per cent level.

questions.stem: Given the excerpt, why does the analyst treat the three comparisons as one family?

options.text: Because they feed a single decision, so their chances of a false positive must be controlled together.
Because they are the only tests that ran that day, so they belong together automatically.
options.misconception: Groups tests by the day they happened

options.text: Because grouping them always makes each individual test more significant.
options.misconception: Believes grouping increases significance

options.text: Because a family lets the analyst report the smallest p-value as the family result.
options.misconception: Believes a family is summarised by its smallest p-value

questions.explanation: Family membership reflects shared decisions: these comparisons together determine the rollout, so their error chances must be controlled jointly. Running them on the same day means nothing and grouping never raises significance.
questions.hint: Group by decision, not by day.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Apply a two-step fix to an inflated family-wise error rate.
questions.stem: A ticket runs eight separate checks and the release notes now fail unpredictably. First state what threshold each check should use, then state what the team gains by making that change.

options.text: Each check should use the family alpha divided by eight, and the chance of any false positive is capped.
Each check should keep the full alpha, and the chance of any false positive is capped.
options.misconception: Keeps the uncorrected threshold while claiming a guarantee

options.text: Each check should use the family alpha multiplied by eight, and the chance of any false positive is capped.
options.misconception: Raises the threshold in the wrong direction

options.text: Each check should report no threshold at all, and the chance of any false positive is capped.
options.misconception: Removes the decision rule while claiming a guarantee

questions.explanation: Dividing the family alpha by the number of checks caps the chance of at least one false positive at the family level, which is what the team wants. Keeping or multiplying the full alpha leaves that risk uncontrolled.
questions.hint: Share one budget across eight checks.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain the trade-off a Bonferroni correction introduces.
questions.stem: A ticket asks what the team gives up when it tightens the threshold for every comparison in a family.

options.text: Statistical power, because the stricter threshold makes real but modest effects harder to detect.
Statistical power, because a stricter threshold makes the tests easier to reject the null.
options.misconception: Believes a stricter threshold rejects the null more often

options.text: The family error rate, because a stricter threshold lets more false positives through.
options.misconception: Believes a stricter threshold admits more false positives

options.text: Interpretability, because the corrected threshold can no longer be reported in full.
options.misconception: Believes the corrected threshold cannot be written down

questions.explanation: A lower threshold means only very large evidence survives, so the method protects the error rate by reducing the chance of detecting genuine modest effects. It never makes rejection easier.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a standardised mean difference in context.
questions.stem: A ticket reports a standardised mean difference of 0.2 between the new and the old upload path. What is the fair reading?

options.text: The new path is a little better, relative to how spread out the measurements were.
The new path is a little better, and 0.2 means 20 per cent of users improved.
options.misconception: Reads the coefficient as a percentage of users

options.text: The new path is a little better, and 0.2 means the change is unlikely to be chance.
options.misconception: Treats a coefficient as a significance verdict

options.text: The new path is a little better, and 0.2 means the interval is narrow and precise.
options.misconception: Treats a coefficient as a statement about precision

questions.explanation: A standardised difference of 0.2 places the gap at a fifth of the shared spread, a modest separation. The figure describes size only, not a user percentage, a significance verdict, or precision.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Compute a within-group sum of squares from a spread and sample size.
questions.stem: A ticket reports that the slower group has 25 members and a within-group standard deviation of 8. What is that group's within-group sum of squares?
questions.explanation: The within-group sum of squares is the sample size minus one multiplied by the variance, so 24 times 64 gives 1536. Using 25 instead of 24, or the standard deviation without squaring it, gives the wrong figure.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain what makes a confidence interval wide or narrow.
questions.stem: A ticket asks for a written explanation of why the interval for one group's estimate is much wider than another's.

answer.exemplar: Interval width is driven by the standard error of the estimate and by the critical value set by the confidence level. A group with a smaller sample or a more dispersed set of measurements has a larger standard error, so the same confidence level produces a wider interval. Because the team used the same confidence level for both groups, the difference must come from their standard errors rather than from the choice of level.

questions.explanation: Width grows with the standard error and with the critical value of the confidence level. Holding the confidence level fixed, a smaller or more dispersed sample gives a larger standard error.
questions.hint: Standard error and the critical value.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Order the steps for computing a correlation from paired records.
questions.stem: A ticket asks for the working order when computing a correlation from paired records. Which sequence starts correctly?

options.text: Compute the sums of x, y, xy, x squared and y squared, then substitute them into the formula.
Convert both variables to percentages, then subtract the mean of x from the mean of y.
options.misconception: Converts the scale before any computation

options.text: Rank the records by x, then count how often y rises in the same order as x.
options.misconception: Uses a rank count instead of the correlation formula

options.text: Multiply x by y for each record, then divide the total by the number of records.
options.misconception: Divides a product sum by the count instead of standardising

questions.explanation: The correlation formula is expressed in terms of summary sums, so those must be collected first and then substituted. Converting to percentages, counting ranks, or dividing a product sum by the count all produce different quantities.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Read a masked trial result for a residual observer effect.

stimulus.body: A trial ticket gives half the participants a build that appears to speed things up and half a build with no visible difference, without telling anyone which is which. The analyst notes that the second group reported more speed than the first.

questions.stem: Given the excerpt, what does the result suggest about the observer effect in this trial?

options.text: There is still an observer effect, since the placebo group reported the larger speed-up.
There is no observer effect, since participants did not know which build they had.
options.misconception: Equates masking with eliminating the effect

options.text: The trial shows the real build is slower, so the new build should be withdrawn.
options.misconception: Reads a reported speed difference as a real performance gap

options.text: The trial proves the placebo build is more effective, so both groups should get it.
options.misconception: Treats the placebo result as proof of superiority

questions.explanation: The trial masked the condition, yet the placebo group still reported the larger speed-up, pointing to an expectation effect. Masking reduces the effect but does not prove it has gone.
questions.hint: Masking reduces, it does not erase.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Apply a two-stage plan to a family of tests.
questions.stem: A ticket lists five families of tests for the release. First state how many comparisons the release contains, then state what has to be fixed before those comparisons can be interpreted.

options.text: All of them, and the family alpha and membership must be settled before any threshold is applied.
Five, and nothing needs fixing because each family carries its own alpha.
options.misconception: Counts families and ignores the need to set error budgets

options.text: All of them, and each family should be corrected only after the first false positive appears.
options.misconception: Waits for an error before setting the correction

options.text: Five, and the release should report one p-value per family instead of per comparison.
options.misconception: Reports one p-value per family, hiding the number of tests

questions.explanation: The release contains one comparison for every test in every family, so all of them count. Before any threshold is applied, the team must fix family membership and the shared family alpha.
questions.hint: Every comparison counts, not every family.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Define the family-wise error rate correctly.
questions.stem: A ticket asks the analyst to state precisely what the family-wise error rate measures for a set of related checks.

options.text: The probability that at least one of the checks wrongly rejects the null hypothesis.
The probability that every one of the checks wrongly rejects the null hypothesis.
options.misconception: Requires every test in the family to fail wrongly

options.text: The probability that the check with the smallest p-value wrongly rejects the null.
options.misconception: Restricts the error to the smallest p-value

options.text: The probability that the average of the checks wrongly rejects the null hypothesis.
options.misconception: Defines the error on an average of the results

questions.explanation: The family-wise error rate is the chance of at least one false positive anywhere in the family, which is why it grows with the number of checks. It is not the chance all checks fail wrongly.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Read the effect of a correction on a single reported result.
questions.stem: A ticket reports a p-value of 0.02 for a test drawn from a family of five at a family alpha of 0.05. How should the analyst read it?

options.text: The corrected threshold is 0.01, so the test no longer reaches significance.
The corrected threshold is 0.10, so the test remains comfortably significant.
options.misconception: Multiplies the alpha by the family size

options.text: The corrected threshold is 0.25, so the test remains comfortably significant.
options.misconception: Multiplies the alpha and then keeps the old verdict

options.text: The corrected threshold is 0.01, so the test becomes more significant than before.
options.misconception: Picks the right threshold but reverses the conclusion

questions.explanation: Dividing the family alpha of 0.05 by five tests gives a per-test threshold of 0.01, and 0.02 no longer clears it. Multiplying the alpha inflates the threshold, and correction never adds significance.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Compute a standardised mean difference from means and a pooled spread.
questions.stem: A ticket reports mean response times of 9.5 seconds and 8.7 seconds for two workflows with a pooled standard deviation of 1.6 seconds. What is the standardised mean difference?
questions.explanation: The mean gap is 9.5 minus 8.7, that is 0.8 seconds, and dividing by the pooled spread of 1.6 gives 0.5. Reversing the ratio or dividing by the means gives a different quantity.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the pooled spread is used when comparing two groups.
questions.stem: A ticket asks the analyst to explain in writing why the comparison uses a single pooled spread taken from both groups.

answer.exemplar: The pooled spread estimates how much the measurements vary around their group means using the evidence from both groups, so it does not rely on one group's own scatter. Using a single spread makes the standardised gap depend on the data rather than on which group happened to be measured more noisily, and it uses every observation available.

questions.explanation: Pooling both groups' variation gives a more stable estimate of scatter than using one group alone, so the standardised gap does not hinge on one noisy arm. It also uses every observation collected.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Order the steps for narrowing a confidence interval.
questions.stem: A ticket asks how the team should work to narrow a confidence interval for the same quantity. Which sequence starts correctly?

options.text: Measure the current standard error, then add observations, then recompute at the same confidence level.
Round the estimate to fewer decimals, then add observations, then report the new interval as narrower.
options.misconception: Uses rounding as if it narrowed the interval

options.text: Choose a higher confidence level, then add observations, then present the result as tighter.
options.misconception: Raises the confidence level while calling the result tighter

options.text: Discard the widest measurements, then add observations, then report the interval without comment.
options.misconception: Trims data without checking what it does to the interval

questions.explanation: The standard error says what to target, and adding observations reduces it, narrowing the interval at the same confidence level. Rounding or trimming changes the report, not the true uncertainty.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Read what a near-zero correlation supports.

stimulus.body: A ticket pairs the number of review comments on a pull request with the number of lines changed, across 40 pull requests. The analyst computes a coefficient of 0.05 and notes that the two quantities are measured on entirely different scales and that no measurement was changed by the review itself.

questions.stem: Given the excerpt, what does a coefficient of 0.05 support?

options.text: Only that the two quantities show almost no linear relationship in this sample.
That review comments have no effect at all on the size of a pull request.
options.misconception: Reads a near-zero coefficient as proof of no effect

options.text: That the two quantities are unrelated because they use different scales.
options.misconception: Believes different scales rule out a relationship

options.text: That the sample size of 40 is too small for any correlation to be trusted.
options.misconception: Blames the sample size for a near-zero result

questions.explanation: A coefficient near zero indicates almost no linear relationship between the two quantities in this sample. It does not prove comments have no effect, and differing scales do not prevent a meaningful correlation.
questions.hint: Near zero means no linear link.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Apply a two-stage fix to an observer effect in a pilot.
questions.stem: A pilot ticket shows that watched participants answer differently from unwatched ones. First name the control condition to add, then name the design change that limits the effect.

options.text: Add a placebo arm with the same ritual, and mask which build each participant receives.
Add more participants to the watched group, and mask which build each participant receives.
options.misconception: Grows the observed group instead of controlling attention

options.text: Add a placebo arm with a shorter session, and tell participants which build they received.
options.misconception: Adds a placebo that differs in ritual and reveals the condition

options.text: Add a second researcher to watch the participants, and mask which build each receives.
options.misconception: Adds more observation instead of removing the effect

questions.explanation: A placebo arm with the same ritual controls for attention and time, and masking the build stops participants guessing their condition. Adding watchers or revealing the build would deepen the effect.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a family of tests from unrelated separate tests.
questions.stem: A ticket asks what makes a set of checks count as one family rather than as unrelated separate tests.

options.text: They share a decision and an error budget, so their false-positive chances must be controlled together.
They all appear in the same sprint, and that alone makes them one family.
options.misconception: Defines a family by the sprint the tests ran in

options.text: They were all run by the same engineer, which ties their errors together.
options.misconception: Defines a family by who ran the tests

options.text: They all produced results that are close to each other in size.
options.misconception: Defines a family by similar result sizes

questions.explanation: A family is a set of comparisons feeding one decision, so their false-positive chances must be controlled jointly. Sharing a sprint, an author, or a similar effect size does not create a family.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Interpret how the number of checks affects false-positive risk.
questions.stem: A ticket contrasts two pipelines: one runs three checks and the other runs twelve, all at the same per-check level. What should the team expect?

options.text: The pipeline with twelve checks has a higher chance of reporting at least one false positive.
Both pipelines carry the same chance, because each check uses the same level.
options.misconception: Equates per-check level with family-wise risk

options.text: The pipeline with three checks has the higher chance, because small groups are noisier.
options.misconception: Confuses sample size effects with the number of comparisons

options.text: Both pipelines are safe, because a per-check level bounds the family risk on its own.
options.misconception: Believes the per-check level bounds the family risk alone

questions.explanation: More independent checks mean more separate chances of a false positive, so the twelve-check pipeline carries the higher family-wise risk. A per-check level bounds a single comparison, not the family.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Compute a corrected per-test significance threshold.
questions.stem: A ticket runs eight comparisons under a family alpha of 0.10 and applies a Bonferroni correction. What threshold should each comparison be judged against?
questions.explanation: The correction divides the family alpha by the number of comparisons, so 0.10 divided by 8 gives 0.0125. Multiplying the alpha instead of dividing it would loosen the threshold and leave the family risk unbounded.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain the value of reporting a standardised mean difference.
questions.stem: A ticket asks the analyst to explain in writing why a standardised mean difference is reported alongside the raw group means.

answer.exemplar: Raw means carry the units of the measurement and cannot be compared with a result from another study that used seconds instead of minutes. Dividing the gap by a common spread gives a unitless number, so a reader can see whether the separation is small, medium or large regardless of the measurement scale, while the raw means stay available for practical decisions.

questions.explanation: Standardising gives a unitless figure comparable with other studies, while raw means stay available for practical decisions. It describes the gap relative to variability, not its absolute size.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Order the steps for obtaining a pooled spread.
questions.stem: A ticket asks for the working order when producing a pooled spread for two groups. Which sequence begins correctly?

options.text: Find each group's variance, weight it by its degrees of freedom, then take the square root.
Add the two standard deviations together, then divide by two and take the square root.
options.misconception: Adds deviations instead of pooling variances

options.text: Average the two variances, then multiply by the total sample size and take the square root.
options.misconception: Uses an unweighted average and the wrong degrees of freedom

options.text: Take the square root of the sum of the two sample sizes, then divide by each variance.
options.misconception: Puts the sample size in the numerator of the formula

questions.explanation: Pooling starts from variances, weights each by its degrees of freedom, then takes the square root to return to the spread scale. Averaging standard deviations mixes scales and gives the wrong value.
questions.hint: Pool the variances, not the deviations.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Read why two groups with equal spread get different interval widths.

stimulus.body: A ticket compares the mean time to resolve a ticket across two teams. Team A has 500 resolutions with a spread of 40 minutes, and team B has 50 resolutions with a spread of 40 minutes. Both intervals use the same confidence level, and Team A's interval comes out noticeably narrower.

questions.stem: Given the excerpt, why is Team A's interval narrower than Team B's?

options.text: Team A has more observations, so its standard error and therefore its interval are smaller.
Team A has more observations, so its spread must be smaller than Team B's spread.
options.misconception: Confuses a smaller standard error with a smaller spread

options.text: Team A has more observations, so its critical value is smaller than Team B's critical value.
options.misconception: Believes sample size changes the critical value

options.text: Team A has more observations, so the team chose a higher confidence level than Team B.
options.misconception: Believes a higher confidence level narrows the interval

questions.explanation: Both teams share the spread and confidence level, so only the standard error differs, and more observations make it smaller. A smaller standard error narrows the interval; the critical value depends on confidence alone.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Apply correlation reasoning in two stages.
questions.stem: A ticket reports a correlation of 0.92 between two measures. First state what the number establishes, then state what it leaves open.

options.text: It establishes a strong linear association here, and it leaves the direction of cause open.
It establishes that the first measure causes the second, and it leaves precision open.
options.misconception: Treats association as causation and mislabels the open question

options.text: It establishes that the two measures are equivalent, and it leaves the sample size open.
options.misconception: Treats correlation as equivalence

options.text: It establishes the association holds in all populations, and it leaves the sign open.
options.misconception: Generalises to all populations and mislabels the open question

questions.explanation: A high coefficient describes a strong linear association within the observed sample and nothing about causation. It also says nothing about generalising to other populations or about the two measures being interchangeable.
questions.hint: Association is established, cause is not.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a placebo effect from an observer effect.
questions.stem: A ticket asks the analyst to separate two things in a trial report that sound very similar.

options.text: A placebo effect comes from expecting treatment; an observer effect comes from being watched.
A placebo effect comes from being watched; an observer effect comes from expecting treatment.
options.misconception: Swaps the two definitions

options.text: A placebo effect and an observer effect are two names for the same reaction to being observed.
options.misconception: Treats the two effects as identical

options.text: A placebo effect comes from the placebo batch itself; an observer effect comes from the notes.
options.misconception: Attributes both effects to material artefacts rather than expectations

questions.explanation: The placebo effect comes from expectation of benefit, while the observer effect comes from awareness of being watched. Blinding addresses the second and a convincing control addresses the first.

options.misconception: Swaps the count of families and comparisons

options.misconception: Excludes a family from the count of tests run

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Compute a family-wise error probability from independent checks.
questions.stem: A ticket runs five independent checks, each at the conventional five per cent level. What is the probability that at least one check reports a false positive?
questions.explanation: All five checks are clean with chance 0.95 to the fifth, about 0.7738, so at least one false positive appears with chance about 0.2262. Adding the five per cent levels wrongly assumes exclusive chances.
questions.hint: One minus the joint clean chance.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a Bonferroni correction bounds the family-wise error rate.
questions.stem: A ticket asks the analyst to explain in writing why dividing the alpha by the number of tests is a guarantee rather than a hope.

answer.exemplar: Each of the k comparisons is judged at alpha divided by k, so each carries at most a one in k chance of a false positive. Summing those chances across the k comparisons gives at most alpha in total, whatever the dependence between them. That is why the bound holds by construction and needs no assumption about how the tests are related.

questions.explanation: Each comparison judged at alpha over k contributes at most a one in k chance of a false positive, and summing over k comparisons caps the total at alpha.
questions.hint: The bound comes from adding the chances.
